output:
**The house in Glenmore — one post from me**

I’m writing this myself, once, so that everyone hears it from me. Úna set this blog up years ago so the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds could keep up with us. I’ve read it more than I’ve written it, but I’d rather use it properly now than have this go round in bits on the phone. I’ve agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore, the old Mulkerrin place where Tom grew up. The closing date is 15 January 2027. I’m putting that date down plainly because some of you heard things second-hand already, and I don’t want anyone hearing any part of this from someone else again.

The house was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. Tom died in March 2024. Since then I’ve been driving out every fortnight, forty minutes each way, to air it and check the pipes. That’s what it’s been: a house to be aired and checked, not a home anymore. That sounds cold. I don’t mean it cold. It’s just what it became. I know the road out there the way I know the back of my hand, and I know the sound the back door makes when it’s stiff. I go in, open the windows, check the pipes, and come home. It’s not a life. It’s a duty, and I’ve been glad to do it, but it’s a duty.

I’m not going to pretend I’ve been brave about it. Some weeks I’ve gone out and sat in the car before I went in. Some weeks I’ve talked to Tom while I was checking the pipes, which is a foolish thing to admit, but there it is. The house has been the last place I could still feel him, and that’s not nothing. But a house isn’t a person, and it isn’t a marriage. It’s a building with a roof that needs €38,000 spent on it.

We agreed the sale on 3 November with Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross. They have two small children. They want to live in it, not run it as a holiday let. The price was fair. It was under what the Dublin crowd offered in the summer. I took the lower one on purpose. I’m not pretending I’m a philanthropist. I wanted a family in it, and I could afford to take less. Not everyone could, and I know that. Some people will think I was foolish to leave money on the table. Maybe I was. But I didn’t want the house to become something with a key safe and a cleaning rota. I wanted children in it. I know there were higher offers. I know some people will say I was mad. Maybe I was. But I’ve seen what happens to places like that when nobody lives in them full-time. They get quiet and damp, and then they get sold again. I wanted it to go to someone who’d put a buggy in the hall and muddy boots by the door.

I know some of you will wonder why now, or why at all. The honest answer is that it isn’t one thing. Ó Flaithearta’s did a roof survey in September. The slates and the back chimney need doing; the quote was €38,000. There’s damp in the back bedroom on top of that. The septic tank needs replacing before it could be sold to anyone anyway. That’s the house as it stands. It isn’t a museum piece. It’s a house that needs a young family’s money and energy, and I don’t have either to give it. I’m not an engineer, but I can read a quote, and I can count.

But it’s not only money. Last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there twenty minutes before I could get up. I told nobody until now. I’m seventy-one. I can still drive and I can still manage my own life, but I can’t manage that house on my own, and I’m afraid of being alone out there since the fall. That’s not a dramatic thing to say. It’s just true. I cannot go on maintaining it. I don’t say that for sympathy. I say it because it’s the reason the house changed from something I could manage to something I was afraid of. I’ve thought since about what would have happened if I’d hit my head, or if the frost had been worse. I don’t like that thought. I don’t like lying in bed at night listening to the house settle and wondering if I’d get up if I fell again. That’s the truth of it. It’s not a dramatic truth. It’s just an old woman’s truth, and I’m not ashamed of it.

I regret not consulting Declan. I should have. He’s the eldest, and he loved that house in a way the rest of you maybe didn’t, or didn’t show. But I am not willing to wait until his summer visit. The house can’t be left another winter the way it is, and I’m not able for another year of driving out to check pipes and lie awake wondering about the roof. I know that sounds stubborn. It is stubborn. I’m not going to pretend I handled it well either. I didn’t. I made a hames of telling people, and I’m sorry for that. I know Declan would have wanted a say. He should have had a say. I’m not going to argue that point. But a say isn’t the same as a veto, and waiting until summer isn’t a plan. The house can’t sit empty for another year while we all think about it. I made the decision I thought was right, and I’ll stand over it, even if I made a mess of telling people.

I love that house. I don’t want anyone thinking I don’t. Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind it in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching. I can still see the cattle looking at us as if we’d lost our minds. The children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan refused to come out until his lips were blue. He was always the stubborn one. I’ve thought about those things a lot. I’ve thought about Tom’s boots by the back door and the way he’d stand at the gate talking to whoever passed. It wasn’t a postcard. It was a working house, with hard winters and bad years as well as good ones. But it was ours. Some of you will have your own memories of the house, and they won’t all be mine. That’s as it should be. A house holds different versions of the same family. I don’t want to write over yours. I’m only telling you mine so you know why I’m not selling it out of carelessness.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I’ve come to think he was right. The Joyces have two small children. I’d be lying if I said that didn’t matter to me. It matters more than the extra money would have. I’m not saying I’m noble. I’m saying I had a choice, and I made the one I could live with. I’m not saying the Joyces are a replacement for Tom, or for us. They’re not. They’re a young family who need a house, and the house needs a young family. That’s all. But it’s not nothing.

It has taken me the best part of two years to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. I didn’t arrive at that quickly. I fought it. I thought selling was a kind of betrayal. Now I think keeping it empty might be the betrayal. I don’t expect anyone else to have reached that on the same timetable. I’m not asking you to agree with me. I’m asking you to hear it from me, and to understand that this isn’t a decision I made lightly or in a hurry. I’m not asking for anyone’s permission. I’m not asking for a vote. I’m asking you to understand that I didn’t do this because I stopped caring. I did it because I couldn’t go on the way things were, and because I think Tom would have understood.

I want you to know what’s being kept. The dresser is going to Úna’s. Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign are staying in the family. I’m not having the place cleared out by strangers and I don’t want anyone picturing that. I’ll make sure those things are safe before the house is emptied. Aoife and Kevin have said that any of the family can come out and walk the land any time. I’m passing that on because I know it matters. They’ve said it themselves, and I’d ask you to take them at their word.

Now the part I got wrong. Declan heard about the sale from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp, not from me. He rang me at two in the morning his time. He said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back I shouldn’t have. I won’t repeat them here. They were said in anger and they’re between the two of us. I’m sorry for how he found out. I’m not sorry for the decision. There’s a difference, and I need him to hear it. I know that’s a hard sentence to read. It’s a hard sentence to write. But if I pretended I was sorry for selling, I’d be lying, and he’d know it.

Declan, I know you read these. I’m not angry with you. I was angry that night, and I said things I shouldn’t have, but I’m not angry now. The door is open. That doesn’t mean I’m going to change my mind. It means you’re my son and you’re welcome in my house, and in this, even if you’re angry with me. Ring me when you’re ready, or don’t, but it’s open. I know you might not want to read this. That’s all right. I’m not writing it to force you to answer. I’m writing it so you know where I stand.

Before the house is cleared, I’d like to have a family day out there. Sunday 13 December. Anyone who can make it, come. I’ll have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies. It won’t be a big production. I just want people to see it one more time, and to be in the same place together before it changes hands. If you can’t make it, I understand. It’s a long way from Perth, and it’s a long way from Boston. But if you can, come. I’ll have the heat on and the kettle boiled. I know December is a busy month. I know some of you are far away. But if you can come, come. If you can’t, ring me after. I’d rather have a phone call than silence.

I’m sorry for how some of you found out. That’s my fault. I’d rather say it all once, honestly, to everyone, than have it go round in bits on the phone. So this is me saying it. The sale closes on 15 January 2027. The day out is Sunday 13 December. I hope to see as many of you as can make it.
